Azul: Stained Glass of Sintra challenges players to carefully select glass panes to complete their windows while being careful not to damage or waste supplies in the process. The window panels are double-sided, providing players with a dynamic player board that affords nearly infinite variability!

Gameplay is similar to Azul.  Players draft colored glass tiles to their player board. Later in the round, players score points based on how they've placed their window pane pieces pieces. Extra points are scored for specific patterns and completing sets.  There's also a new Colour Bonus mechanic at the end of every round for additional scoring strategy. The game will come to an end after 6 rounds. The player with the most points at the end of the game wins.

Azul: Stained Glass of Sintra has new components including translucent window pane pieces, a tower to hold discarded glass panes, and double-sided player boards and window pane panels.

—description from the publisher

[Rating: 1/10] This is one of those games that I disliked from the very first round. Gameplay is so extremely boring and unengaging that I had a problem finishing it, every minute was absolute pain. I didn't care what was happening, I just wanted it to end. I hate it and will never play it again.

[Rating: 1/10] Just an alright variant twist on Azul, all the new mechanical and scoring features here are fairly interesting but all these changes to the system lead to the player interaction being less pronounced which is what I found made the original Azul stand out from similar tile laying games. As a result, Stained Glass of Sintra isn't a game I find compelling enough to choose to play over some of its alternatives.

[Rating: 1/10] The most horrible excruciating, horrible, terrifying experience a boardgame could offer. Literally no one at the table was happy, not even the winner. Do not play unless you've got some masochist longings.  My main gripe: I usually enjoy player interaction, but here it's reduced to taking the stones another player wanted, throwing off their plans and forcing them to think off an entirely new one. As a result, the game crawls ahead at snail's pace as you can only really start planning your turn once it's already your turn - no planning ahead allowed. One of my life goals is to buy a home and replace every single light bulb with a smart LED bulb that color shifts toward orange then red at night.  I'm not sure if "games that I can only play in the middle of the day using light with good color-rendering" is acceptable.
